Nearly unrelatedly: a few months back I tried to have Qwen and all the frontier models be a RISCV CPU, and they all failed miserably every time. They'd get a handful of instructions in at most before derailing completely. What surprised me the most was that they would all often fail on decoding instructions, which should be pretty close to a task that they've shown themselves to be good at before.

I even added a warmup phase where they were given the answer to a decode and a few steps of running, and ask them to abort if they disagreed. Didn't help.

All in all, for someone who doesn't use LLMs much, this was a far more exhausting and boring exercise than I'd imagine it to be. The only thing that sparked some joy was the models' persistent cheating, whereby they'd try to analyze the whole program upfront and only give the final output (when applicable), despite orders to faithfully step through each and every instruction.
With RAM prices what they are, I'm glad we've found a way to turn LLMs back into RAM.

If I understand this clearly enough, what they really did was

A) add a post-processor which accepted a decoded tool call specifying what the processor should invoke.

B) had the post-processor perform the computation in tensor space.

The kv-cache/activations were not shared between qwen/the processor which is how they avoided fine tuning etc. I'm not clear how the tensor representation benefited the computation in this pipeline.
